To scrimp means to spend as little money as possible, or to use as little of something as possible — usually because money is tight, or because you're working hard toward a financial goal. It's about cutting back on your needs and comforts to make ends meet or to save up.

Picture someone who eats very plain meals, buys nothing new, skips entertainment, and carefully counts every penny they spend. That person is scrimping.

Scrimping is not just "being careful with money." There's a strong sense of effort and sacrifice in it. When you scrimp, you're not casually choosing the cheaper option — you're actively denying yourself things you want or even need. Life feels tight. This is what separates it from a neutral word like save. Saving sounds responsible and pleasant. Scrimping sounds harder — it suggests you're really stretching things thin, possibly out of necessity.

You'll very often hear scrimp paired with save: "scrimp and save." This means to live very frugally over a long period in order to build up money. The two words strengthen each other — you scrimp (sacrifice and cut back) so that you can save (accumulate money).

"My grandparents scrimped and saved for twenty years to buy their home."

When you scrimp on something specific, it means you spend too little on it or use too little of it — often in a way that hurts the quality or result.

  • "Don't scrimp on the paint — cheap paint peels quickly."
  • "She scrimped on the ingredients and the cake didn't taste right."

Notice that in this usage, scrimping is presented as a mistake — something that backfires. You can scrimp too much, and the result suffers.

The word can swing either way depending on context.

Positively — when a person scrims out of genuine need or for a worthy goal, we feel sympathy or admiration: "They scrimped and saved for years to give their children a better life."

Negatively — when a company or authority scrims in a way that causes harm or failure, it feels like irresponsibility or greed: "The contractor scrimped on materials, and the roof collapsed within a year."
How It Differs from Similar Words

Skimp is the word closest to scrimp, and the two are often used interchangeably. The subtle difference: skimp on tends to focus on giving or providing too little to others (a restaurant skimping on portions), while scrimp tends to focus more on personal sacrifice and cutting back on one's own life. In practice, most native speakers use them almost identically.

Economize means to reduce spending in a calm, organized way. It's more neutral — no suffering implied, just smart planning.

Penny-pinch means to be obsessively and unreasonably tight with money, usually to the frustration of others. It's more negative in tone than scrimp.

Be frugal means to live simply and avoid waste as a deliberate, positive lifestyle choice. Frugal people are seen as wise and disciplined — not suffering. Scrimping, by contrast, often implies hardship rather than a free choice.

To scrimp is to cut back sharply — on spending, on comfort, on things you'd otherwise enjoy — usually because you have little money, or because you're sacrificing now for something important later. It carries weight. It implies real effort. And when someone or something scrims on a specific thing, it usually means they've gone too far — the result is noticeably worse for it.
